parole.significato: Forms feminine nouns from masculine nouns.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic -ъка (-ŭka), from Proto-Slavic *-ъka.

parole.significato: Forms nouns that indicate the action or result of a verb
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic -ѣль (-jělĭ), reanalyzed as plural, from Proto-Slavic *-ělь.

parole.significato: Forms adjectives and nouns indicating origin or place of birth (such as from a certain city or region), or occasionally…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic -ѣнинъ (-jěninŭ), from Proto-Slavic *-ěninъ. Might also be conflated with Latin -iānus.

parole.significato: noun suffix used to denote a place
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic -ище (-ište), from Proto-Slavic *-išče.

parole.significato: Used to make feminine forms of some masculine nouns, e.g. professions; -ess
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic -ица (-ica), from Proto-Slavic *-ica.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic агода (agoda), from Proto-Slavic *agoda.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic видомъ (vidomŭ, “visible”), from Proto-Slavic *vidomъ, from *vidъ. Another theory suggests Latin ad idem.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ꙗвѣ (javě), from Proto-Slavic *aviti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic баба (baba), from Proto-Slavic *baba (“old woman”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic баснь (basnĭ), from Proto-Slavic *basnь.

parole.significato: a bizarre thing, an unbelievable thing
parole.testo: From earlier form bezaconie, borrowed from Old Church Slavonic безакониѥ (bezakonije), from Proto-Slavic *bez (“without”) + *zakonъ (“law”) + *-ьje (denominal, forming collective nouns).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic безъчьстьникъ (bezŭčĭstĭnikŭ), from безъ- (bezŭ-) + чьсть (čĭstĭ) + -ьникъ (-ĭnikŭ), from Proto-Slavic *bez- (“without”) + *čьstь (“honor”) + *-nikъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic без (bez), from Proto-Slavic *bez.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic бездъна (bezdŭna), from Proto-Slavic *bezdъna.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic бичь (bičĭ), from Proto-Slavic *bičь.

parole.significato: ex-, former (preceding a medieval rank in Wallachia or Moldavia)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic бꙑвъ (byvŭ), from Proto-Slavic *byvъ (“former”), from *byti (“to be”).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic бꙑволъ (byvolŭ), from Proto-Slavic *byvolъ, from Vulgar Latin *būvalus, from Latin būbalus, from Ancient Greek βούβαλος (boúbalos). Doublet of bour, which was inherited from Latin.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic благочьстивъ (blagočĭstivŭ), from чьсть (čĭstĭ), from Proto-Slavic *čьstь.

parole.significato: soft, shy, silly, dull, weak, foolish, sheepish
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic благъ (blagŭ), from Proto-Slavic *bolgъ (“good”). Compare Serbo-Croatian blag.

parole.significato: dish, bowl, container or receptacle for food
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic блюдо (bljudo), from Proto-Slavic *bľudo.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic боль (bolĭ), from Proto-Slavic *bolь. Compare Serbo-Croatian bol.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic богатъ (bogatŭ), from Proto-Slavic *bogatъ.
From the given name Bogdan, from Old Church Slavonic Богъданъ (Bogŭdanŭ), from Proto-Slavic *Bogъdanъ. Named after Bogdan I, the founder of Moldavia.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic бодль (bodlĭ), from Proto-Slavic *bodъľь (“needle, pointy tip”). Compare Bulgarian бодил (bodil).

parole.significato: to ail (to be ill; to suffer; to be troubled)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic болѣти (bolěti), from Proto-Slavic *bolěti. By surface analysis, boală + -i.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic бразда (brazda), from Proto-Slavic *borzda.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic братрьство (bratrĭstvo), from Proto-Slavic *bratrьstvo (brotherhood).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic бебръ (bebrŭ), from Proto-Slavic *bebrъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic боукъварь (bukŭvarĭ), from боукꙑ (buky, “letter”), from Proto-Slavic *buky. Compare Serbo-Croatian буквар (“primer”), Macedonian буквар (bukvar, “primer”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic божоуръ (božurŭ), from Proto-Slavic *božurъ (“peony”). Compare Macedonian божур (božur), Old Hungarian bazsár.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic бꙑльѥ (bylĭje, “plant, herb”), from Proto-Slavic *bylьje.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic бърлогъ (bŭrlogŭ), from Proto-Slavic *bьrlogъ, *bьrloga. Compare Bulgarian бърлога (bărloga), Serbo-Croatian brlog (“den, lair”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic брьвьно (brĭvĭno), from Proto-Slavic *brьvьno.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic бътъ (bŭtŭ), from Proto-Slavic *bъtъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic *бездꙑханиѥ (*bezdyxanije), from без- (bez-) + дꙑхати (dyxati) + -аниѥ (-anije), from Proto-Slavic *dyxati (“to breathe”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic бѣжаниѥ (běžanije, “escape”), from бѣжати (běžati) + -аниѥ (-anije), from Proto-Slavic *běžati (“to flee, to escape”).
From băl, from Old Church Slavonic бѣлъ (bělŭ), from Proto-Slavic *bělъ (“white”) or Albanian balë.
From bâlie + -ărie, from Old Church Slavonic бꙑльѥ (bylĭje, “plant, herb”), from Proto-Slavic *bylьje.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic казнь (kaznĭ), from Proto-Slavic *kaznь (“punishment”); Compare Serbo-Croatian kazna.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic часъ (časŭ), from Proto-Slavic *časъ (“time”).

parole.significato: group, band, gang, pack, troop, flock
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic чета (četa), from Proto-Slavic *četa.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic чашникъ (čašnikŭ), from Proto-Slavic *čašnikъ, from *čaša (“cup”) + *-nikъ (forms agents). Compare Czech číšník (“waiter”), Polish cześnik (“cupbearer”), Russian чашник (čašnik, “cupbearer”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic чрьнити (črĭniti), from Proto-Slavic *črъnìti (“to blacken”), from *čь̀rnъ (“black”). Compare Serbo-Croatian цр́нети /cŕneti, Russian черни́ть (černítʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic чьсть (čĭstĭ), from Proto-Slavic *čьstь, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kʷit-tis.

parole.significato: to revere, honor, esteem, respect, pay homage to
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic чьстити (čĭstiti), form of чьтити (čĭtiti, “to respect”), from Proto-Slavic *čьstiti.

parole.significato: bone, usually large, with or without meat on it
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic члѣнъ (člěnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *čelnъ (“member, part”). Compare Bulgarian член (člen, “member, limb”), Serbo-Croatian члан (“member”), Czech člen (“member”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic четврьтъ (četvrĭtŭ, “quarter”), from Proto-Slavic *četvьrtъ. Compare Bulgarian четвърт (četvărt).

parole.significato: herd, flock, drove (of cattle or other horned animals)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic чрѣда (črěda), from Proto-Slavic *čerda (“herd, flock”), from Proto-Indo-European *kerdʰ-. Doublet of cârd and ciurdă. Compare (obsolete) Serbo-Croatian čreda, Russian череда́ (čeredá, “sequence, train”), English herd.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic читати (čitati), from Proto-Slavic *čitati (“speak aloud words written”), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeyt-.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic чюдо (čjudo), from Proto-Slavic *čudo.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic клеветати (klevetati), from Proto-Slavic *klevetati. Compare Serbo-Croatian klevetati.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic клѣщѧ (klěštę), from Proto-Slavic *klěšča. Compare Aromanian cleashti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic клепати (klepati), from Proto-Slavic *klepati.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic клокотъ (klokotŭ), from Proto-Slavic *klokotъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic клокотати (klokotati), from Proto-Slavic *klokotati.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic клопотъ (klopotŭ), from Proto-Slavic *klopotъ.

parole.significato: person in charge with supplying the royal court
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ключарь (ključarĭ, “keykeeper”), from ключь (ključĭ, “key”), from Proto-Slavic *kľučь (“key”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic клатити (klatiti), from Proto-Slavic *koltiti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic кънѧжьна (kŭnęžĭna, “princess”), from кънѧѕь (kŭnędzĭ, “prince”), from Proto-Slavic *kъnędzь (“prince”). Doublet of Chiajna.

parole.significato: ruler of a state or principality in past times
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic кънѧзь (kŭnęzĭ, “prince”), from Proto-Slavic *kъnędzь (“prince”), borrowed from Proto-Germanic *kuningaz. The latter sense was influenced by Russian князь (knjazʹ) and Ukrainian князь (knjazʹ). Doublet of chinez.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic коса (kosa), from Proto-Slavic *kosa. Compare Bulgarian коса (kosa), Serbo-Croatian коса, Russian коса (kosa), Albanian kosë, Aromanian coasã.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic кокошь (kokošĭ), from Proto-Slavic *kokošь. Compare Serbo-Croatian kokoš and Bulgarian кокош (kokoš).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic кожоухъ (kožuxŭ), from Proto-Slavic *kožuxъ, from Proto-Slavic *koža (“leather”). Compare Serbo-Croatian kožuh, Polish kożuch, Slovak kožuch, Russian кожух (kožux).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic колачь (kolačĭ), from Proto-Slavic *kolačь. Cognates include Bulgarian колач (kolač), Czech koláč, Polish kołacz, Serbo-Croatian kolač, Russian калач (kalač).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic колѧда (kolęda), from Proto-Slavic *kolęda, itself from Latin kalendae, calendae. The Latin word probably left a lost or unattested Romanian word *cărinde (compare related word cărindar), which influenced or became crossed with the Slavic-derived version to make the
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic кольць (kolĭcĭ), from колъ (kolŭ) + -ьць (-ĭcĭ), from Proto-Slavic *kolъ. Compare Bulgarian колец (kolec), Serbo-Croatian kòlac.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic коньць (konĭcĭ), from Proto-Slavic *konьcь. Compare Russian конец (konec), Bulgarian конец (konec), Czech konec.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic копыто (kopyto), from Proto-Slavic *kopyto.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic корабль (korablĭ), from Proto-Slavic *korabľь, from Byzantine Greek καράβιν (karábin), from Ancient Greek καράβιον (karábion) or κάραβος (kárabos, “boat, crab, beetle”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic косити (kositi), from Proto-Slavic *kositi.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic косорь (kosorĭ), from Proto-Slavic *kosorь.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic котьць (kotĭcĭ), from Proto-Slavic *kotьcь.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ковачь (kovačĭ), from Proto-Slavic *kovačь (“smith”), from *kovati (“to forge”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic кошь (košĭ), from Proto-Slavic *košь. Compare Bulgarian кош (koš, “basket”), Slovak kôš (“basket”).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ковьчегъ (kovĭčegŭ), from Proto-Slavic *kovъčegъ, from Middle Mongol ᠬᠠᠭᠤᠷᠴᠠᠭ (qagurčaɣ) presumably through a Turkic language. Compare Mongolian хуурцаг (xuurcag), Bulgarian ковчег (kovčeg), Serbo-Croatian kovčeg.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic кошьница (košĭnica), diminutive of кошь (košĭ), from Proto-Slavic *košь (“basket”). Compare Bulgarian кошница (košnica), Macedonian кошница (košnica).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic крал҄ь (kralʹĭ), from Proto-Slavic *korľь. Compare Bulgarian крал (kral), Serbo-Croatian kralj.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic краи (krai), from Proto-Slavic *krajь (“edge”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic крастѣль (krastělĭ), from Proto-Slavic *korstělь. Compare Bulgarian крастел (krastel), Russian коростель (korostelʹ), Czech chřástal, Slovak chriašteľ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic крѫгъ (krǫgŭ), from Proto-Slavic *krǫgъ. Doublet of crug.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic коупьць (kupĭcĭ), from Proto-Slavic *kupьcь (“trader”), from Proto-Slavic *kupiti (“to purchase”), from Proto-Germanic *kaupōną (“to buy”), from *kaupô (“merchant”), from Latin caupo (“merchant, innkeeper, shopkeeper”). Compare Ukrainian купець (kupecʹ), Slovak kupe
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic кръчьма (krŭčĭma), from Proto-Slavic *kъrčьma. Compare Bulgarian кръчма (krăčma), Serbo-Croatian krčma, Polish karczma.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic кръмити (krŭmiti), from Proto-Slavic *kъrmiti, from *kъrma (“helm”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic кръма (krŭma), from Proto-Slavic *kъrma, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷr-m-. Compare Serbo-Croatian krma (“stern”).

parole.significato: short, small, and with a raised tip; snub-nosed
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic крънъ (krŭnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *kъrnъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic кръпа (krŭpa), from Proto-Slavic *kъrpa. Compare Aromanian cãrpã, Serbo-Croatian krpa.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic кадити (kaditi), from Proto-Slavic *kaditi.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic каꙗти (kajati), from Proto-Slavic *kajati.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic каꙗнъ (kajanŭ), past participle of каꙗти (kajati), from Proto-Slavic *kajati (“to repent, to regret”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic калити (kaliti, “to harden”), from Proto-Slavic *kaliti. Compare Serbo-Croatian kaliti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic калина (kalina), from Proto-Slavic *kalina. Compare Russian кали́на (kalína) and Polish kalina.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic даръ (darŭ), from Proto-Slavic *darъ (“gift”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic дѣдина (dědina), from Proto-Slavic *dědina.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic дѣлъ (dělŭ), from Proto-Slavic *dělъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic дꙑхание (dyxanije), from Proto-Slavic *dyxanьje, from *dyxati (“to breathe”). Compare Bulgarian дихание (dihanie).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic дъхорь (dŭxorĭ), from Proto-Slavic *dъxorь. Compare Macedonian твор (tvor, “skunk”), Slovene dihur (“polecat”), Russian хорь (xorʹ).

parole.significato: to get, acquire, gain, find, achieve, secure, obtain, procure
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic добꙑти (dobyti), from Proto-Slavic *dobyti, from *do- + *byti.
From the verb dobândi, from Old Church Slavonic добꙑти (dobyti), from Proto-Slavic *dobyti, from *do- + *byti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic догорѣти (dogorěti), from до- (do-) + горѣти (gorěti, “to burn”), from Proto-Slavic *gorěti.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic догънати (dogŭnati), from гънати (gŭnati), from Proto-Slavic *gъnati. Cognates include Bulgarian догоня (dogonja), Russian догонять (dogonjatʹ, “to chase, to catch up”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic домолити (domoliti), from до- (do-) + молити (moliti), from Proto-Slavic *modliti.

parole.significato: to prove, to demonstrate; to vindicate
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic довѣдѣти (dověděti), from до- (do-, “completely”) + вѣдѣти (věděti, “to know”), from Proto-Slavic *věděti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic драгъ (dragŭ), from Proto-Slavic *dorgъ. Bulgarian драг (drag).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic драгость (dragostĭ), from Proto-Slavic *dorgostь, from *dorgъ + *-ostь.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic дроужьба (družĭba), from Proto-Slavic *družьba.
Learned borrowing from Old Church Slavonic доухъ (duxŭ), from Proto-Slavic *duxъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic доухнѫти (duxnǫti), from Proto-Slavic *duxnǫti, from *duxъ (“spirit, breath, smell”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic дѫбьць (dǫbĭcĭ), from дѫбъ (dǫbŭ) + -ьць (-ĭcĭ), from Proto-Slavic *dǫbъ (“oak”) + *-ьcь.

parole.significato: young or small forest; thicket, coppice, grove
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic дѫбрава (dǫbrava), from Proto-Slavic *dǫbrava.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic дѫга (dǫga), from Proto-Slavic *dǫga.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic дворъ (dvorŭ), from Proto-Slavic *dvòrъ.

parole.significato: to serve at the royal court or a noble
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic дворити (dvoriti), from Proto-Slavic *dvoriti, from *dvorъ (“court”). Compare Serbo-Croatian dvoriti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic дрьзъ (drĭzŭ), from Proto-Slavic *dьrzъ (“daring”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic дира (dira), from Proto-Slavic *dira.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic даровати (darovati), from Proto-Slavic *darovati, from *darъ (“gift”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic хвала (xvala), from Proto-Slavic *xvala.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic свѣтило (světilo, “lamp”), from свѣтъ (světŭ) + -ило (-ilo), from Proto-Slavic *světъ (“light”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic хвалити (xvaliti), from Proto-Slavic *xvaliti, from *xvala.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic гиздавъ (gizdavŭ), from Proto-Slavic *gyzdavъ, from *gyzdъ + *-avъ. Compare Bulgarian гиздав (gizdav), Serbo-Croatian gizdav, Polish gizdawy.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic глаголъ (glagolŭ), from Proto-Slavic *golgolъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic гласъ (glasŭ, “voice”), from Proto-Slavic *golsъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic глезьнь (glezĭnĭ), from Proto-Slavic *gleznъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic глоба (globa), from Proto-Slavic *globa.

parole.significato: a crowd, mass, mob, herd, multitude (sometimes with a pejorative sense, as in rabble, commoners, simple people)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic глота (glota), from Proto-Slavic *glota. Compare Serbo-Croatian glota, Polish gołota (“the poor”). Doublet of holotă.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic глоумъ (glumŭ), from Proto-Slavic *glumъ.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic голъ (golŭ), from Proto-Slavic *golъ (“naked”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gelH- (“naked, bald”). Compare Bulgarian гол (gol), Serbo-Croatian go, gol, Ukrainian го́лий (hólyj).

parole.significato: to chase away, cast out, banish, drive away, drive out, hound out
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic гонити (goniti, “to chase”), from Proto-Slavic *goniti.

parole.significato: householder; master of the house or head of a household
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic господарь (gospodarĭ), from Proto-Slavic *gospodařь, ultimately from *gospodь.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic господинъ (gospodinŭ), from Proto-Slavic *gospodinь.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic граждь m (graždĭ), from Proto-Slavic *gorďь; compare Bulgarian гражд (gražd).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic граница (granica), from Proto-Slavic *granica (“boundary, border”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic гребенъ (grebenŭ), from Proto-Slavic *greby.

parole.significato: to err, to do wrong, to mistake
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic грѣшити (grěšiti), from Proto-Slavic *grěšiti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic грѧда (gręda), from Proto-Slavic *gręda. Compare Serbo-Croatian greda.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic гривна (grivna), from Proto-Slavic *grivьna.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic гроза (groza), from Proto-Slavic *groza. Compare Bulgarian гроза (groza), Serbo-Croatian groza.

parole.significato: to hurry, be in a rush, make haste
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic грабити (grabiti), from Proto-Slavic *grabiti. Compare Bulgarian грабя (grabja).

parole.significato: a mass, heap, pile, multitude, lot of something
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic грамада (gramada), from Proto-Slavic *gromada. Compare also Albanian gërmadhë.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic гнои (gnoi), from Proto-Slavic *gnojь. Compare Serbo-Croatian гној, Russian гной (gnoj).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic гноище (gnoište), from гнои (gnoi) + -ище (-ište), from Proto-Slavic *gnojь (“manure”) + Proto-Slavic *-išče (“place of”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic хлъмъ (xlŭmŭ), from Proto-Slavic *xъlmъ, from a Germanic language, possibly Gothic; cf. Proto-Germanic *hulmaz. Cognate with Swedish holm.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic *глътъ (*glŭtŭ) (hence Bulgarian гълтам (găltam, “to swallow”)), from Proto-Slavic *gъltъ, related to *glъtati (“to swallow, devour”). Compare also gât.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic гѫгнанѥ (gǫgnanje), from гѫгнати (gǫgnati), from Proto-Slavic *gǫgnati (“to speak through the nose”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic гѫгавъ (gǫgavŭ), from Proto-Slavic *gǫgnavъ (“speaking through the nose”).
Metathesis of older gâltej (Dosofteiu), derivative of gâlt + -ej (modern gât), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic глътъ (glŭtŭ), from Proto-Slavic *gъltъ, related to *glъtati (“to swallow, devour”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic хмель (xmelĭ), from Proto-Slavic *xъmelь. Compare Bulgarian хмел (hmel), Serbo-Croatian хме̏љ, Russian хмель (xmelʹ), Polish chmiel.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic храмъ (xramŭ), from Proto-Slavic *xormъ. Compare Russian храм (xram), Bulgarian храм (hram), Macedonian храм (hram), and Serbo-Croatian храм (hrȃm). For usage as patron saint's day, compare Ukrainian храм (xram).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic храна (xrana), from Proto-Slavic *xorna.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic хрѣнъ (xrěnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *xrěnъ. Compare Bulgarian хрян (hrjan).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic хранити (xraniti), from Proto-Slavic *xorniti. Compare hrană.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic рꙑльць (rylĭcĭ), from Proto-Slavic *rylьcь, from *ryti (“to dig”) + *-ьcь (forms agent nouns). Cognates include Polish rylec (“stylus”), Slovene rilec.

parole.significato: artificial lake made by damming a river
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ѣзъ (jězŭ), from Proto-Slavic *ězъ (“weir”). Cognates include Bulgarian яз (jaz), Serbo-Croatian jaz, Czech jez, Polish jaz.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic любовьникъ (ljubovĭnikŭ), from Proto-Slavic *ľubovьnikъ, from *ľubỳ.

parole.significato: spawn, roe, fish eggs in general
parole.testo: From the singular icră, from Old Church Slavonic икра (ikra), from Proto-Slavic *jьkrā, from Proto-Indo-European *ikʷ(e)r- (“fish egg”). Compare Russian икра́ (ikrá), Serbo-Croatian ikra.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ꙗсли (jasli), from Proto-Slavic *jasli. Compare Bulgarian ясла (jasla), Russian ясли (jasli), Serbo-Croatian јасле.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ѥзеро (jezero), from Proto-Slavic *ezero.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic исходити (isxoditi, “to go out”), from Proto-Slavic *isxoditi, from *xoditi.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съпасъ (sŭpasŭ, “savior”), from Proto-Slavic *sъ(n) + *pasti (“to pasture, herd”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic исправа (isprava), from Proto-Slavic *jьzprava, from *pravъ. Compare Bulgarian изправа (izprava).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съпасти (sŭpasti, “to save, to redeem from eternal damnation”), from Proto-Slavic *sъ(n) + *pasti (“to pasture, herd”). Compare Serbo-Croatian spasiti, Czech spasit, Russian спасти (spasti).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic истьць (istĭcĭ), from Proto-Slavic *jьstьcь.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic любити (ljubiti), or directly from Proto-Slavic *ľubiti. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *lewbʰ-.

parole.significato: fast (occurring or happening within a short time)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic лютъ (ljutŭ), from Proto-Slavic *ľutъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ꙗвити (javiti), from Proto-Slavic *javiti, from *aviti (“to show”).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic избити (izbiti), from из- (iz-) + бити (biti), from Proto-Slavic *biti (“to beat”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeyH-. Compare Serbo-Croatian izbiti and Russian избить (izbitʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic избѫдѫ (izbǫdǫ), from избꙑти (izbyti), from Proto-Slavic *jьzbyti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic избавити (izbaviti), from из- (iz-) + бавити (baviti), from Proto-Slavic *baviti.

parole.significato: to chase away, chase off, drive away, banish, expel
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic изгонити (izgoniti), from Proto-Slavic *jьzgoniti. Compare Serbo-Croatian izgoniti.

Plural of izmană, borrowed from Old Church Slavonic измѣна (izměna), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *měniti (“to change”). Compare Serbo-Croatian izmena (“change”). For the semantic evolution from "change", compare Italian mutande.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic измѣнити (izměniti), from Proto-Slavic *izměniti (“to change”), from *měniti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic изворъ (izvorŭ), from Proto-Slavic *jьzvorъ, from *verti. Compare Aromanian izvur.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic жаль (žalĭ), from Proto-Slavic *žalь. Compare Aromanian jali.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic жаръ (žarŭ), from Proto-Slavic *žarъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic жєгъ (žegŭ), from Proto-Slavic *žegъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic желаниѥ (želanije), from Proto-Slavic *želanije, from *želěti. Compare Russian желание (želanije), Bulgarian желание (želanie).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic жалити (žaliti), from Proto-Slavic *žaliti. Compare Bulgarian жаля (žalja), Serbo-Croatian žaliti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic жаловати (žalovati), from Proto-Slavic *žalovati, from *žaliti (“to grieve”), from *žalь (“sorrow”). Compare Polish żałować.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic жрьтва (žrĭtva), from Proto-Slavic *žьrtva.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic жлѣбъ (žlěbŭ) (via a form *ž(g)leb), from Proto-Slavic *želbъ. Compare Serbo-Croatian žlijeb/žleb.

From the regionalism jid + -an, from Old Church Slavonic жидъ (židŭ), from Proto-Slavic *židъ, ultimately from Ancient Greek Ἰουδαῖος (Ioudaîos) and Hebrew יהודי (Yehudi); see also Russian жид (žid), Serbo-Croatian žid, Ukrainian жид (žyd).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic жидовинъ (židovinŭ), from Proto-Slavic *židъ, from Old Italian giudeo, from Latin iūdaeus. For the sense of "giant", see the similar sense found in Proto-Slavic, perhaps due to biblical stories and the idea of the Jews being the first people, combined with the Roman

parole.significato: to covet, crave, yearn or long for
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic жѧдати (žędati), from Proto-Slavic *žędati.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic житьница (žitĭnica), from Proto-Slavic *žitьnica, from *žito (“grain”). Compare Russian житница (žitnica), Bulgarian житница (žitnica), Serbo-Croatian žitnica.

parole.significato: medieval title in Wallachia and Moldavia
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic жоупанъ (županŭ), from Proto-Slavic *županъ (“lord”), from Proto-Slavic *župa (“district”). Doublet of jupân.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic жоупаница (županica), from Proto-Slavic *županica, from *županъ (“lord”), from *župa (“district”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic лакомъ (lakomŭ), from Proto-Slavic *olkomъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic льнъ (lĭnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *lьnъ. Compare Ukrainian лан (lan).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic лѣкъ (lěkŭ), from Proto-Slavic *lěkъ, from Proto-Germanic *lēkijaz.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic лѣто (lěto), from Proto-Slavic *lěto.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic лебедь (lebedĭ), from Proto-Slavic *olbǫdь. Compare Bulgarian лебед (lebed), Russian лебедь (lebedʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic лиꙗти (lijati), from Proto-Slavic *lijati (“to pour”), from *liti (“to pour”). The meaning was "as if poured into a mold", hence its derivation from "to pour".
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic лѣнь (lěnĭ), from Proto-Slavic *lěnь. Compare Serbo-Croatian lijénōst, Russian лень (lenʹ), Polish leń. Cf also Aromanian leani.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic любовь (ljubovĭ), from Proto-Slavic *ľuby.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic лѣпити (lěpiti), from Proto-Slavic *lěpiti, from Proto-Indo-European *leyp- (“to stick”). Compare also Aromanian alãchescu, alichescu.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic лоза (loza), from Proto-Slavic *loza (“vine”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic лобода (loboda), from Proto-Slavic *loboda.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic лагодинъ (lagodinŭ), from Proto-Slavic *lagodinъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic лопата (lopata), from Proto-Slavic *lopata.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ловити (loviti), from Proto-Slavic *loviti. Compare Serbo-Croatian loviti; cf. also Megleno-Romanian luves (“hunt”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic лѫка (lǫka), from Proto-Slavic *lǫka (“water-meadow”). Cognates include Bulgarian лъка (lăka), Serbo-Croatian luka.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic *макъ (*makŭ), from Proto-Slavic *makъ (“poppy”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic мѣнити (měniti, “to think”), from Proto-Slavic *měniti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic мѣзинъ (mězinŭ), from Proto-Slavic *mězinъ. A derivation from Latin mediānus is improbable. Cognates include Russian мизинный (mizinnyj).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic медъ (medŭ), from Proto-Slavic *mȅdъ, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *médʰu.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic миловати (milovati), from Proto-Slavic *milovati, from *milъ (“nice, gentle”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic милъ (milŭ), from Proto-Slavic *milъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic мѧчь (męčĭ), from Proto-Slavic *męčь (“ball”). Compare Russian мяч (mjač).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic мꙑто (myto), from Proto-Slavic *myto. Compare Bulgarian мито (mito, “tax”), Serbo-Croatian мито (“bribe”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic младъ (mladŭ), from Proto-Slavic *moldъ (“youth”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic млащина (mlaština), from Proto-Slavic *molka. Doublet of mlacă.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic мощи (mošti), from Proto-Slavic *moťь.

parole.significato: to smolder, to simmer (about a fire)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic мокнѫти (moknǫti), from Proto-Slavic *moknǫti (“to become wet”). Compare Russian мокнуть (moknutʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic моль (molĭ), from Proto-Slavic *moľь.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic молитва (molitva), from Proto-Slavic *modlitva.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic молитва (molitva), from Proto-Slavic *modlitva.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic молотрь (molotrĭ), from Proto-Slavic *molotrь.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic мамити (mamiti), from Proto-Slavic *mamiti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic мора (mora), from Proto-Slavic *mora, with suffix + -oi.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic смрадьница (smradĭnica), from смрадьнъ (smradĭnŭ, “stinky”), from смрадъ (smradŭ, “stench”), from Proto-Slavic *smordъ (“stench”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic мрѣжа (mrěža), from Proto-Slavic *merža. Compare Serbo-Croatian mreža.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic мѫчити (mǫčiti, “to torture”), from Proto-Slavic *mǫčiti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic мѫка (mǫka), from Proto-Slavic *mǫka (“torture, torment”), compare Serbo-Croatian muka.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic мльчати (mlĭčati), from Proto-Slavic *mьlčati (“to be silent”).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic мѫдръ (mǫdrŭ, “wise”), from Proto-Slavic *mǫdrъ, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *mondʰh₁ros, from *men(s)dʰh₁- + *-rós. Compare Polish mądry, Russian мудрый (mudryj).

parole.significato: to dirty, soil, sully, taint, begrime, tarnish
parole.testo: Possibly from Old Church Slavonic мажѫ (mažǫ), first person singular indicative present of мазати (mazati), from Proto-Slavic *màzati.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic мѣзга (mězga), from Proto-Slavic *mězga. Cognate with Polish miazga, Czech míza, Russian мезга (mezga, “vegetable pulp”).
From mâzgă, from Old Church Slavonic мѣзга (mězga), from Proto-Slavic *mězga.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic маслина (maslina), from масло (maslo, “oil, butter”) + -ина (-ina), from Proto-Slavic *maslo. Compare Aromanian mas(i)nã, Serbo-Croatian maslina.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic нетрѣбьнъ (netrěbĭnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *netrĕbьnъ, from *ne- (“non-”) + *trĕbъ (“labour”) + *-ьnъ (adjectival suffix).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic невѣста (nevěsta), from Proto-Slavic *nevěsta.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic невольнъ (nevolĭnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *nevolьnъ, from *ne- (“non-”) + *volъ (“sufficiency”) + *-ьnъ (adjectival suffix).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic наковало (nakovalo), from Proto-Slavic *nakovalo.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic нарокъ (narokŭ, “sentence”), from на- (na-) + рокъ (rokŭ), from Proto-Slavic *rokъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic народъ (narodŭ), from Proto-Slavic *narodъ. Doublet of nerod.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic надежда (nadežda), from Proto-Slavic *nadeďa. Compare Bulgarian надежда (nadežda).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic напасть (napastĭ), from Proto-Slavic *napastь. Cognates include Russian напасть (napastʹ).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic напраснъ (naprasnŭ, “sudden, quick”), from Proto-Slavic *naprasьnъ. Compare Bulgarian напрасен (naprasen), Serbo-Croatian naprasan, Ukrainian напрасний (naprasnyj), Russian напрасный (naprasnyj). By surface analysis, năprasnă + -ic.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic напоустити (napustiti), from поустити (pustiti), from Proto-Slavic *pustiti (“to let, let go”). Compare Macedonian напушти (napušti).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic напасти (napasti, “to attack”), from на- (na-) + пасти (pasti), from Proto-Slavic *pasti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic напастовати (napastovati), from Proto-Slavic *napastь.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic нъравъ (nŭravŭ, “temperament, character”), from Proto-Slavic *norvъ (“habit”). Cognates include Bulgarian нърав (nărav), Russian нрав (nrav), Serbo-Croatian нарав, Polish narów.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic насильнъ (nasilĭnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *nasilьnъ, from *na- + *sila (“force”) + *-ьnъ. Compare Russian насильный (nasilʹnyj).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic нетѧгъ (netęgŭ), from Proto-Slavic *netęgъ (“lazy person”). Compare Russian нетяг (netjag).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic неоукъ (neukŭ), from Proto-Slavic *neukъ (“untaught”), from *učiti (“to teach”). Compare Bulgarian неук (neuk), Macedonian неук (neuk, “ignorant”), Serbo-Croatian neuk (“ignorant”), Serbo-Croatian nieuk (“dunce”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic неводъ (nevodŭ), from Proto-Slavic *nevodъ. Compare Serbo-Croatian navod.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic назьрѣти (nazĭrěti), from на- (na-) + зьрѣти (zĭrěti), from Proto-Slavic *zьrěti (“to observe”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic обꙑчаи (obyčai), from Proto-Slavic *obyčajь. Compare Serbo-Croatian ȍbičāj/о̏бича̄ј, Russian обы́чай (obýčaj).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic область (oblastĭ), from Proto-Slavic *obolstь.

parole.significato: to treat a sick person; to bandage a wound
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic обложити (obložiti), from Proto-Slavic *obložiti (“to cover”), from *ob- + *ložiti (“to lay”). Compare Serbo-Croatian obložiti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic обьлъ (obĭlŭ), from Proto-Slavic *obьlъ (“round”). Cognates include Russian облый (oblyj), Bulgarian объл (obăl), Polish obły.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic облѫкъ (oblǫkŭ), from об- (ob-) + лѫкъ (lǫkŭ, “bow”), from Proto-Slavic *lǫkъ. Compare Aromanian ublãncu, blãncu, cf. Slovene oblúk.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic образъ (obrazŭ), from Proto-Slavic *obrazъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic обѧтрити (obętriti), from Proto-Slavic *obъjętriti, from *ob- + *jętriti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic обьщь (obĭštĭ, “common”), from Proto-Slavic *obьťь.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic отьче нашь (otĭče našĭ), from Proto-Slavic *otьcь (“father”) + *našь (“our”).

parole.significato: a piece of land with hereditary property rights
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic отьцина (otĭcina), from Proto-Slavic *otьcina, from *otьcь (“father”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic окно (okno), from Proto-Slavic *okъno (“window”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic около (okolo), from Proto-Slavic *okolo, from *kolo.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic отраслъ (otraslŭ), from Proto-Slavic *otraslъ. Compare Russian отрасль (otraslʹ, “branch”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic одежда (odežda), from Proto-Slavic *odeďa.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic одѣꙗло (odějalo, “coverlet, outwear”), from Proto-Slavic *odějadlo, from *odeďa. Compare Bulgarian одеяло (odejalo).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic оглѧдати (oględati, “to glance”), from Proto-Slavic *oględati (cf. Polish oglądać, Russian глядеть (gljadetʹ)).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic угоръ (ugorŭ), from Proto-Slavic *ugorъ. Compare Bulgarian угар (ugar), Serbo-Croatian ugar.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ограда (ograda, “enclosure”), from Proto-Slavic *o(b)gorda, from *gorďь (“fence”). Compare Russian огород (ogorod, “vegetable garden”).

parole.significato: inula, elecampane (Inula spp., especially Inula helenium)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic оманъ (omanŭ), from Proto-Slavic *omanъ.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic оморити (omoriti), variant of оуморити (umoriti), from Proto-Slavic *umoriti. Compare Serbo-Croatian umoriti. First attested in the 1500s, in the oldest Romanian texts.

parole.significato: to stop the movement of something
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic опрѣти (oprěti), from о- (o-) + пьрѣти (pĭrěti), from Proto-Slavic *perti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic оурѧдити (uręditi), from рѧдъ (rędŭ), from Proto-Slavic *rędъ (“row”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ось (osĭ), from Proto-Slavic *osь (“axle”). Cognates include Bulgarian ос (os), Russian ось (osʹ), Serbo-Croatian os, Czech osa, Polish oś. Doublet of ax and axă.

parole.significato: to tire, tire out, become tired, weary, worn out, fatigued, etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic оустанѫ (ustanǫ, “I stop”), from оустати (ustati, “to cease, to stop”), from стати (stati, “to stand”), from Proto-Slavic *stati.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic островъ (ostrovŭ), from Proto-Slavic *ostrovъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic осѫдити (osǫditi), from Proto-Slavic *sǫditi (“to judge”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic отьць (otĭcĭ), from Proto-Slavic *otьcь.
A Slavic borrowing replacing the inherited (now obsolete) term toapsec. Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic отрава (otrava), from Proto-Slavic *otrava. Compare Russian отрава (otrava), Czech otrava.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic овесъ (ovesŭ), from Proto-Slavic *ovьsъ. Compare Aromanian uvedz, Bulgarian ове́с (ovés), Serbo-Croatian òvas.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic оцьтъ (ocĭtŭ), Proto-Slavic *ocьtъ, from Gothic 𐌰𐌺𐌴𐌹𐍄 (akeit) or 𐌰𐌺𐌴𐍄 (akēt), from Latin acetum. Compare Serbo-Croatian ocat, Bulgarian оцет (ocet).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пакость (pakostĭ, “madness, tyranny”), from Proto-Slavic *pakostь (“vicissitude”). Cognates include Russian пакость (pakostʹ), Ukrainian па́кість (pákistʹ), Belarusian па́косць (pákoscʹ), Bulgarian па́кост (pákost, “harm”), Serbo-Croatian pȁkōst (“malice”), Slovene
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пагоуба (paguba), from Proto-Slavic *paguba.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пашище (pašište), from пасти (pasti) + -ище (-ište) from Proto-Slavic *pasti (“to graze”) + *-išče (“place of”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic печать (pečatĭ), from Proto-Slavic *pečatь.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic печатьлѣти (pečatĭlěti), from Proto-Slavic *pečatьlěti, from *pečatь (“seal”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic периѥ (perije), from перо (pero, “feather”) + -иѥ (-ije), from Proto-Slavic *pero.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пьстрꙑ (pĭstry), from Proto-Slavic *pьstrъ (“multicolored”). Compare Russian пёстрый (pjóstryj), Czech pestrý, Polish pstry. Doublet of păstrăv.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пещера (peštera), from Proto-Slavic *peťera, from *peťь (“oven”) + *-era. Compare Bulgarian пещера (peštera).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пила (pila), from Proto-Slavic *pila, from Old High German fil (“file”).
From pistru (“regional term describing a sheep with black spots on its head”), from Old Church Slavonic пьстръ (pĭstrŭ), from Proto-Slavic *pьstrъ.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пивьница (pivĭnica), from пиво (pivo, “beer”) + -ьница (-ĭnica), from Proto-Slavic *pivo. Compare Slovak pivnica, Serbo-Croatian pivnica, Polish piwnica, Hungarian pince.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пизда (pizda), from Proto-Slavic *pizda (“vulva”). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *písdeh₂. Compare Russian пизда́ (pizdá), Polish pizda.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пласа (plasa), from Proto-Slavic *polsa.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic плата (plata), from Proto-Slavic *plata. Also compare Serbo-Croatian plata (“pay”), Russian плата (plata, “fee, pay”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic плѣнъ (plěnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *pelnъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic плѣвы (plěvy), from Proto-Slavic *pelva. Compare Macedonian плева (pleva), Serbo-Croatian плева.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic плѣшь (plěšĭ), from Proto-Slavic *plěšь. Cognates include Czech pleš, Russian плешь (plešʹ).

parole.significato: tribute paid by Wallachia and Moldavia to the Ottoman Empire, recognizing Ottoman suzerainty
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic поклонъ (poklonŭ), from Proto-Slavic *poklonъ (“bowing”), from *klonъ. Compare Polish pokłon (“obeisance”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic поклонити (pokloniti), from Proto-Slavic *pokloniti (“to bow”), from *poklonъ (“bow”), from *klonъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic плодъ (plodŭ), from Proto-Slavic *plodъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic плодити (ploditi), from Proto-Slavic *ploditi. Cognates include Serbo-Croatian ploditi, Czech plodit, Polish płodzić.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic плотоунъ (plotunŭ), from Proto-Slavic *plotunъ.
Probably from Old Church Slavonic *площьница (*ploštĭnica), from плоскъ (ploskŭ, “wide”) + -ьница (-ĭnica), from Proto-Slavic *ploskъ. Compare Czech ploštice.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic плоугъ (plugŭ), from Proto-Slavic *plugъ, of Germanic origin.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic платити (platiti), from Proto-Slavic *platiti. Compare Aromanian plãtescu.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic полъ (polŭ), from Proto-Slavic *polъ. Compare Serbo-Croatian pola, Russian пола́ (polá), Polish poła, Czech pulka, Bulgarian пола́ (polá).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic починокъ (počinokŭ), from Proto-Slavic *počinъkъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic покаꙗти (pokajati, “to repent”), from Proto-Slavic *kajati.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic подъ (podŭ), from Proto-Slavic *podъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic подъгориѥ (podŭgorije), from Proto-Slavic *podъ (“under”) + *gora (“mountain, hill”) + *-ьje (denominal suffix).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic подъножиѥ (podŭnožije), from Proto-Slavic *podъnožije, from *podъ- (“under”) + *noga (“foot”) + *-ьje. Compare Polish podnóżek, Czech podnožka, Serbo-Croatian podnožje, Bulgarian подножие (podnožie), Russian подножие (podnožije).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic подоба (podoba), from Proto-Slavic *podoba. Compare Serbo-Croatian podoba.

parole.significato: military requisition of transport means from peasants (in Moldavia and Wallachia)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic подъводъ (podŭvodŭ), from Proto-Slavic *voditi. Compare Russian подвод (podvod).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic похътѣти (poxŭtěti), from по- (po-) + хътѣти (xŭtěti), from Proto-Slavic *xъtěti, alternative form of *xotěti (“to want”).
From the verb pofti, from Old Church Slavonic похътѣти (poxŭtěti), from по- (po-) + хътѣти (xŭtěti), from Proto-Slavic *xъtěti, alternative form of *xotěti (“to want”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic *полꙗна (*poljana), from Proto-Slavic *poľana.
Derived from Old Church Slavonic поꙗта (pojata), from Proto-Slavic *pojata through Albanian pojatë. Compare Serbo-Croatian pojata, Hungarian pajta.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пожаръ (požarŭ), from Proto-Slavic *požarъ (“fire”), from *po- + *žarъ.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic похъвица (poxŭvica), diminutive of похъва (poxŭva), from Proto-Slavic *poxъva (“sheath, scabbard”). Cognates include Polish pochwa, Belarusian похва (póxva), Czech pochva, Slovak pošva.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic полица (polica), from Proto-Slavic *polica.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic поминати (pominati, “to remember, to commemorate”), from Proto-Slavic *pomineti. Compare Polish wspomnieć (“to mention, to remember”), Russian помина́ть (pominátʹ, “to commemorate”), Ukrainian помина́ти (pomynáty, “to remember”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic поноръ (ponorŭ), from Proto-Slavic *nora (“abyss”). Compare Bulgarian понор (ponor), Serbo-Croatian ponor.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic поносъ (ponosŭ), from Proto-Slavic *ponosъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic попрѣти (poprěti), from Proto-Slavic *poprěti, from *pьrěti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic порѫчити (porǫčiti), from Proto-Slavic *porǫčiti.

parole.significato: thick, usually homespun cloth, often used in making coats or blankets
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic поставъ (postavŭ), from по- (po-) + ставъ (stavŭ), from Proto-Slavic *stavъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic постельникъ (postelĭnikŭ), from Proto-Slavic *posteljь (“bed”). Compare Russian постельничий (postelʹničij), Ukrainian Постільничий (Postilʹnyčyj).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic потъкнѫти (potŭknǫti), from Proto-Slavic *potъknǫti (“to stumble”).

parole.significato: to soothe, pacify, appease, mitigate, assuage, calm
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic *потолити (*potoliti), from Proto-Slavic *toliti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic потопъ (potopŭ), from Proto-Slavic *potopъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic потопеньѥ (potopenĭje), from потопъ (potopŭ), from Proto-Slavic *potopъ (“flood”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic потопити (potopiti), from Proto-Slavic *potopiti, from *potopъ (“flood”). Compare Serbo-Croatian потопити, Czech potopit.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic противьникъ (protivĭnikŭ, “enemy”), from Proto-Slavic *protivьnikъ (“opponent”), from *protivъ (“against”) + *-nikъ (deverbal suffix).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic поварьнꙗ (povarĭnja), from Proto-Slavic *povarьňa (“kitchen”), from *variti (“to cook”). Compare Russian поварня (povarnja, “kitchen”).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic повѣсть (pověstĭ, “tale, narration, legend”), from Proto-Slavic *pověstь, from *po- + *věstь (“message”). Compare Serbo-Croatian povest (“history”) and Russian повесть (povestʹ, “narrative, story”), Czech pověst (“narrative story”).
From earlier prah, from Old Church Slavonic прахъ (praxŭ), from Proto-Slavic *porxъ, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pers-. Compare Serbo-Croatian prah, also Megleno-Romanian prau.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прагъ (pragŭ), from Proto-Slavic *porgъ (“threshold”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *parˀgas, from Proto-Indo-European *porg-o-. Compare Macedonian праг (prag), Serbo-Croatian prȁg.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прапоръ (praporŭ), from Proto-Slavic *porporъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic правильнъ (pravilĭnŭ), from правило (pravilo, “rule”), from Proto-Slavic *pravъ (“right”). By surface analysis, pravilă + -nic.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic правило (pravilo), from Proto-Slavic *pravidlo (“right”).

parole.significato: meal after a dead person's burial and funeral in their honor/memory; wake; burial feast, funeral repast
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic праздьникъ (prazdĭnikŭ), from праздьнъ (prazdĭnŭ) + -икъ (-ikŭ), from Proto-Slavic *porzdьnъ; compare Serbo-Croatian praznik, Ukrainian празник (praznyk).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic праща (prašta), from Proto-Slavic *porťa (“sling”).

parole.significato: prefix added to adjectives or verbs to indicate exaggeration; over-
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣ- (prě-), from Proto-Slavic *per-.

parole.significato: to hand over, to give in custody an object
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣдати (prědati), from Proto-Slavic *perdati, from *per- (“over, through”) + *dati (“to give”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣдъсловиѥ (prědŭslovije), from прѣдъ (prědŭ, “before”) + слово (slovo, “word”), from Proto-Slavic *perdъ (“before”) + *slovo (“word”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣображениѥ (prěobraženije), from прѣобразити (prěobraziti, “to transform”), from образъ (obrazŭ, “image”), from Proto-Slavic *obrazъ (“image”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣсадити (prěsaditi), from прѣ- (prě-) + садити (saditi), from Proto-Slavic *per- + *saditi (“to plant”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣбѣгъ (prěběgŭ), from Proto-Slavic *prěběgъ, from *běgъ (“to escape”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣчьстьна (prěčĭstĭna), feminine of прѣчьстьнъ (prěčĭstĭnŭ), from чьсть (čĭstĭ, “honor”), from Proto-Slavic *čьstь.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣдати (prědati), from Proto-Slavic *prędati (“to jump”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic притворъ (pritvorŭ), from Proto-Slavic *pritvorъ. Compare Russian притвор (pritvor).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic приꙗтель (prijatelĭ), from Proto-Slavic *prijateľь, from Proto-Indo-European *priH- (“dear”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пригонити (prigoniti), from при- (pri-) + гонити (goniti), from Proto-Slavic *goniti (“to chase, to persecute”).

parole.significato: to be beneficial, favourable, make for good conditions
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic приꙗти (prijati), from Proto-Slavic *prijati. Compare Serbo-Croatian prijati.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣмѣнити (prěměniti), from Proto-Slavic *prěměniti, from *měniti (“to change”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣстолъ (prěstolŭ), from прѣ- (prě-) + столъ (stolŭ), from Proto-Slavic *stolъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣставити (prěstaviti), from прѣ- (prě-) + ставити (staviti), from Proto-Slavic *staviti.

parole.significato: to look, gaze, regard, watch, behold
parole.testo: From older form prăvi, borrowed from Old Church Slavonic правити (praviti), from Proto-Slavic *praviti (“to twist, to turn”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic подъградиѥ (podŭgradije, “suburb”), from подъ (podŭ, “under”) + градъ (gradŭ, “city”), from Proto-Slavic *podъ + *gordъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic простъ (prostŭ), from Proto-Slavic *prostъ.

parole.significato: sand or gravel found on the bottom of bodies of water or within the Earth's crust
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѫдъ (prǫdŭ), from Proto-Slavic *prǫdъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прьстъ (prĭstŭ), from Proto-Slavic *pьrstъ (“finger”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прьстень (prĭstenĭ), from Proto-Slavic *pьrsty.

parole.significato: to fry (to cook in hot fat)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пражити (pražiti), from Proto-Slavic *pražiti. Compare Ukrainian пряжити (prjažyty), Serbo-Croatian pražiti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прасити (prasiti), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *porsę (“piglet”). Compare Bulgarian прася (prasja).

parole.significato: to knock down, throw down, overthrow
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic провалити (provaliti), from про- (pro-) + валити (valiti), from Proto-Slavic *valiti. Compare Serbo-Croatian provaliti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic праздьновати (prazdĭnovati), from праздьнъ (prazdĭnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *porzdьnъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прашити (prašiti), from Proto-Slavic *poršiti, compare with praf. Compare also Aromanian prãshescu.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic поустꙑни (pustyni), from Proto-Slavic *pustyni, from *pustъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic поустиньникъ (pustinĭnikŭ), from поустꙑни (pustyni, “wilderness”) + -ьникъ (-ĭnikŭ), from Proto-Slavic *pustyni (“wilderness”), from *pustъ (“empty”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пькълъ (pĭkŭlŭ), from Proto-Slavic *pьkъlъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic плъкъ (plŭkŭ), from Proto-Slavic *pъlkъ, an early borrowing from Proto-Germanic *fulką.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic плъниѥ (plŭnije, “flow, stream”), from Proto-Slavic *pъlniti (“to fill”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пѫдарь (pǫdarĭ), from Proto-Slavic *pǫditi (“to chase”).

parole.significato: to watch, lurk, wait for, lie in wait, lie in ambush, spy
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пѫдити (pǫditi), from Proto-Slavic *pǫditi.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пръга (prŭga), from Proto-Slavic *pьrga.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пьрѣти (pĭrěti), from Proto-Slavic *pьrěti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic плъхъ (plŭxŭ), from Proto-Slavic *pьlxъ, possibly from Proto-Balto-Slavic *peliā, from Proto-Indo-European *pelH-.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic *паѭжина (*pajǫžina), from паѫкъ (paǫkŭ) + -ина (-ina), from Proto-Slavic *paǫkъ. Compare Aromanian pangu, Bulgarian паяжина (pajažina).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic палити (paliti), from Proto-Slavic *paliti. Compare Serbo-Croatian paliti. Also found in Aromanian as pãlescu, probably indicating an early borrowing.

parole.significato: to guard, watch over, take care of, protect
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пазити (paziti), from Proto-Slavic *paziti. Compare Aromanian pãzescu.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ракъ (rakŭ), from Proto-Slavic *rakъ. Compare Serbo-Croatian rak, Czech rak, Polish rak.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic рай (raj), from Proto-Slavic *rajь, borrowed from Iranian, from Proto-Iranian *raHíš, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *raHíš, from Proto-Indo-European *reh₁ís (“wealth, goods”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic рана (rana), from Proto-Slavic *rana. Compare Serbo-Croatian rana, Bulgarian рана (rana), Russian рана (rana). cf. also Aromanian aranã, ranã.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic робъ (robŭ), from Proto-Slavic *orbъ (“slave”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃órbʰos (“orphan”). Doublet of orb, which was inherited from Latin.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic работа (rabota), from Proto-Slavic *orbota. Doublet of robot.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic родъ (rodŭ), from Proto-Slavic *rodъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic родити (roditi), from Proto-Slavic *roditi.

parole.significato: sedge (Carex), greater pond sedge (Carex riparia) or true fox-sedge (Carex vulpina)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic рогоз (rogoz), from Proto-Slavic *rogozъ. Compare also Aromanian arugoz.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic рои (roi), from Proto-Slavic *rojь. Compare Czech roj, Slovak roj and Serbo-Croatian roj.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic родъ (rodŭ), from Proto-Slavic *rodъ.

parole.significato: laundry (that which needs to be, is, or has been laundered)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic роухо (ruxo), from Proto-Slavic *ruxo. Compare Bulgarian рухо (ruho), Serbo-Croatian ruho.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic роумѣнъ (ruměnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *ruměnъ (“ruddy”). Compare Bulgarian румен (rumen), Serbo-Croatian rumen.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic роусъ (rusŭ), from Proto-Slavic *rusъ. Compare Aromanian arus.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic рѧдъ (rędŭ, “row, line”), from Proto-Slavic *rędъ. Compare also Albanian rend.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic рꙑсь (rysĭ), from Proto-Slavic *rysь. A widely perpetrated false etymology links it to its homonym, claiming that the animal is named for the laughter-like vocalisations.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic рътъ (rŭtŭ), from Proto-Slavic *rъtъ. Compare Bulgarian рът (răt) and Russian рот (rot).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic рогачь (rogačĭ), from Proto-Slavic *rogačь.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ранити (raniti, “to wound”), from Proto-Slavic *raniti, from *rana (“wound”). Compare Aromanian arãnescu, arãniri.

parole.significato: indicates that the action of a verb is repeated or goes back to the preceding situation
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic раз- (raz-), from Proto-Slavic *orz-, with some cases possibly based on Latin re- + ex-; compare Old French res- and its modern reflex, ré-.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic распѫдити (raspǫditi, “to scatter”), from рас- (ras-) + пѫдити (pǫditi), from Proto-Slavic *pǫditi. Less likely from a Vulgar Latin root *reexpandīre (compare French répandre (“to spread, scatter”)), from expandere.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic распѫтиѥ (raspǫtije), from Proto-Slavic *orzpǫtьje. Compare Russian распутье (rasputʹje).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic растѧгнѫти (rastęgnǫti), from рас- (ras-) + тѧгнѫти (tęgnǫti), from Proto-Slavic *tęgnǫti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic развити (razviti), from Proto-Slavic *orzbiti. Compare Serbo-Croatian razbiti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic разбои (razboi), from Proto-Slavic *orzbojь. Compare Serbo-Croatian razboj (“warfare, combat”), Russian разбой (razboj, “robbery”). Cf. also Aromanian arãzboi.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic разбоиникъ (razboinikŭ, “robber”), from Proto-Slavic *orzbojьnikъ. Compare Bulgarian разбойник (razbojnik), Serbo-Croatian razbojnik (“outlaw, bandit”), Russian разбойник (razbojnik, “highwayman, robber”). By surface analysis, război + -nic.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic развратити (razvratiti, “to deviate from the path”), from раз- (raz-, “change”) + вратити (vratiti, “to turn”), from Proto-Slavic *vortiti (“to turn”).

parole.significato: plants sprouted without being purposely planted, from the seeds falling on the ground at harvest
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic самораслъ (samoraslŭ), from Proto-Slavic *samoorstlъ, from *samъ (“self”) + *orsti (“to grow”). Compare Serbo-Croatian samorast.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic скоба (skoba), from Proto-Slavic *skoba.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic скопити (skopiti), from Proto-Slavic *skopiti (“to castrate”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сковрада (skovrada), from Proto-Slavic *skovorda (“frying pan”). Compare Russian сковорода (skovoroda).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic скѫпъ (skǫpŭ), from Proto-Slavic *skǫpъ (compare Serbo-Croatian skȗp, Slovene skôp, Bulgarian скъп (skăp)). Compare Aromanian scumpu.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic скѫдъ (skǫdŭ), from Proto-Slavic *skǫdьnъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic скръбь (skrŭbĭ, “grief, sorrow”), from Proto-Slavic *skъrbь.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic скврънавъ (skvrŭnavŭ, “polluted, unclean, impure”), from сквръна (skvrŭna, “dirt, filth”) + -авъ (-avŭ), from Proto-Slavic *skvьrna.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic скврьна (skvrĭna), from Proto-Slavic *skvьrna. Cognates include Bulgarian скверен (skveren), Russian скверна (skverna), Megleno-Romanian scrămă.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съвада (sŭvada, “quarrel”), from Proto-Slavic *svarъ (“quarrel, strife”).

parole.significato: a strong smell or smoke resulting from burning meat or fat, or a wax candle, etc., or any strong, heavy smoke or odor
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сквара (skvara), from Proto-Slavic *skvara.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съвѣтъ (sŭvětŭ), from Proto-Slavic *sъvětъ. The variant sveat is the most conservative from which all other variants derive. Compare Serbo-Croatian savet. Doublet of soviet.
From older șfert, borrowed from Old Church Slavonic четврьтъ (četvrĭtŭ), from Proto-Slavic *četvьrtъ. Compare Serbo-Croatian četvrt, Ukrainian чверть (čvertʹ).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съвѣтьникъ (sŭvětĭnikŭ), from Proto-Slavic *sъvětьnikъ, from *sъvětъ (“council”) + *-nikъ, from *větъ (“talk, agreement”). Compare Russian советник (sovetnik), Bulgarian съветник (săvetnik), Macedonian советник (sovetnik), Serbo-Croatian savetnik. Piecewise doublet

parole.significato: to be shy, to be intimidated
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic свѣнити (svěniti), from Proto-Slavic *svěniti (“be shy”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съхль (sŭxlĭ, “brushwood”), from Proto-Slavic *sъxlь.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic силити (siliti), from Proto-Slavic *sila (“force”).

parole.significato: abandoned village, place where a village existed.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic селище (selište), from Proto-Slavic *selište, from Proto-Slavic *selo (“village”) + Proto-Slavic *-ište (“place of”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сильнъ (silĭnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *silьnъ (“strong”), from *sila (“strength”) + *-ьnъ (adjectival suffix).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic силовати (silovati), from Proto-Slavic *silovati, from *sila (“force”). Compare Serbo-Croatian silovati (“to force, to rape”).

parole.significato: disgust, loathing, abhorrence, hatred, aversion, antipathy, revulsion, dislike, ill-will, (deep) grudge
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сила (sila), from Proto-Slavic *sila (“force, power, strength”). Compare Aromanian silã, Bulgarian сила (sila), Serbo-Croatian sila.
From Old Church Slavonic сꙑнъ (synŭ), from Proto-Slavic *synъ (“son”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сито (sito), from Proto-Slavic *sito. Compare Bulgarian сито (sito), Serbo-Croatian sito, Polish sito, Aromanian sitã, Albanian sitë.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic слабъ (slabŭ), from Proto-Slavic *slàbъ. Compare Aromanian slab, Bulgarian and Macedonian слаб (slab), Serbo-Croatian slȁb.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic слатина (slatina), from Proto-Slavic *soltina (“salt marsh”), from *solь (“salt”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic слава (slava), from Proto-Slavic *slava.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сълиꙗти (sŭlijati), from Proto-Slavic *sъlijati, from *lijati (“to pour”), from *liti (“to pour”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic свободь (svobodĭ), from Proto-Slavic *svoboda (“freedom”). Compare Bulgarian свободен (svoboden).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic словѣнинъ (slověninŭ). Doublet of sloven. Cf. also șcheau and slav.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic слово (slovo), from Proto-Slavic *slovo.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic слоуга (sluga), from Proto-Slavic *sluga. Compare Serbo-Croatian sluga.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic слоужьба (služĭba), from Proto-Slavic *služьba. Compare Serbo-Croatian služba.

parole.significato: to officiate, perform the functions of some office
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic слоужити (služiti), from Proto-Slavic *služiti. Compare Serbo-Croatian služiti, Czech sloužit.
From slujnic + -ă, from Old Church Slavonic слоужьникъ (služĭnikŭ), from Proto-Slavic *služьnikъ, from *služiti (“to serve”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сланина (slanina), from Proto-Slavic *solnina, from *solnъ (“salt”) + *-ina. Compare Bulgarian сланина (slanina), Serbo-Croatian slanina.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic славити (slaviti, “to praise, to glorify”), from Proto-Slavic *slaviti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic смѣдъ (smědŭ), from Proto-Slavic *smědъ (“brown”). Compare Serbo-Croatian smeđ, Czech snědý.

parole.significato: to be humble, submissive or respectful
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съмѣрити (sŭměriti), from съ- (sŭ-) + мѣрити (měriti, “to measure”), from Proto-Slavic *měriti (“to measure”), from *měra (“measure”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съмѧсти (sŭmęsti), from съ- (sŭ-) + мѧсти (męsti), from Proto-Slavic *męsti (“stir, trouble”).

parole.significato: pitch (dark, extremely viscous material made by distilling tar)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic смола (smola), from Proto-Slavic *smola.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic смокъвинъ (smokŭvinŭ), from смокꙑ (smoky), from Proto-Slavic *smoky, perhaps from Gothic 𐍃𐌼𐌰𐌺𐌺𐌰 (smakka). Compare Bulgarian смокиня (smokinja), Serbo-Croatian smokva.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic смучити (smučiti, “to crawl”), from Proto-Slavic *smučati. Cognates include Slovene smučati (“to ski”).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съметана (sŭmetana), from Proto-Slavic *sъmetana; possibly an early borrowing to explain for the vowel sound change before nasals. The "n" can be explained by the influence of *sъmęsti. Compare Bulgarian сметана (smetana), Russian сметана (smetana).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic смръкати (smrŭkati), from Proto-Slavic *smъrkati. Compare Czech smrkat, Polish smarkać, Russian сморкать (smorkatʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic смрадъ (smradŭ, “stench”), from Proto-Slavic *smьrdъ, from *smьrděti (“to stink”). Compare, Serbo-Croatian smrad, Czech smrad.
From earlier iznoavă, from Old Church Slavonic изъ нова (izŭ nova, “again”), from Proto-Slavic *jьz *novъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic снопъ (snopŭ), from Proto-Slavic *snopъ.
Learned borrowing from Old Church Slavonic съборъ (sŭborŭ), from Proto-Slavic *sъborъ (“meeting, gathering”). Doublet of zbor.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сомъ (somŭ), from Proto-Slavic *somъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сърокъ (sŭrokŭ), from Proto-Slavic *sъrokъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic споръ (sporŭ), from Proto-Slavic *sporъ.
From spor, from Old Church Slavonic споръ (sporŭ), from Proto-Slavic *sporъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съпасениѥ (sŭpasenije), from Proto-Slavic *sъpasenьje. Cognates include Serbo-Croatian spasenje.

parole.significato: shady place where cattle rest during the midday heat
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic станище (stanište), from станъ (stanŭ) + -ище (-ište), from Proto-Slavic *stanъ (“camp”). Compare Serbo-Croatian stanište.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic стѣна (stěna), from Proto-Slavic *stěna.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic старость (starostĭ), from Proto-Slavic *starostь (“old age”), from *starъ (“old”). Compare Russian староста (starosta, “bailiff, village elder, churchwarden”), Polish starosta (“leader”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ставило (stavilo), from ставити (staviti) + -ило (-ilo), from Proto-Slavic *staviti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic стѣгъ (stěgŭ), from Proto-Slavic *stěgъ. Compare Ukrainian стяг (stjah) or Russian стяг (stjag).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic стькло (stĭklo), from Proto-Slavic *stьklo, from Gothic 𐍃𐍄𐌹𐌺𐌻𐍃 (stikls).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic стогъ (stogŭ), from Proto-Slavic *stogъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic стража (straža), from Proto-Slavic *storža. Compare Serbo-Croatian straža.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic страшьнъ (strašĭnŭ, “terrible, horrible, feared”), from Proto-Slavic *strašьnъ (“terrible, frightening”), from *straxъ (“terror, fear”) + *-ьnъ (adjectival suffix).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic стрѣшина (strěšina), from стрѣха (strěxa) + -ина (-ina), from Proto-Slavic *strěxa (“roof”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сътрывати (sŭtryvati), from съ- (sŭ-) + трывати (tryvati), from Proto-Slavic *tryvati (“to scrub”), from *tryti (“to rub”).
Probably from Old Church Slavonic съкропити (sŭkropiti), from съ- (sŭ-) + кропити (kropiti, “to sprinkle”), from Proto-Slavic *kropiti. Compare Ukrainian скропити (skropyty, “to sprinkle”).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic строугъ (strugŭ), from Proto-Slavic *strugъ. Compare Bulgarian струг (strug), Serbo-Croatian strug, Polish strug, Russian струг (strug). The nasal infix may be due to the influence of Greek.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic строуна (struna), from Proto-Slavic *struna (“string”). Cognates include Bulgarian струна (struna), Russian струна (struna), Serbo-Croatian струна, Czech struna, Polish struna, Slovak struna.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic страданиѥ (stradanije), from Proto-Slavic *stradanьje. Compare Bulgarian страдание (stradanie), Russian страдание (stradanije), Serbo-Croatian stradanje.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic страдати (stradati), from Proto-Slavic *stradati (“to suffer”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic стлъпъ (stlŭpŭ, “pillar, column, tower”), from Proto-Slavic *stъlpъ, alternative form of *stъlbъ. Compare Russian столп (stolp).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic стрькъ (strĭkŭ), from Proto-Slavic *stьrkъ. Compare Serbo-Croatian štȓk, Macedonian штрк (štrk), Bulgarian щъ́ркел (štắrkel), Aromanian stircu, also Albanian shtërg.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic соулица (sulica), from Proto-Slavic *sudlica.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съблазнь (sŭblaznĭ, “temptation”), from съ- (sŭ-) + блазнь (blaznĭ), from Proto-Slavic *blaznь (“bait”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic садити (saditi), from Proto-Slavic *saditi (“to plant”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic таинъ (tainŭ), from Proto-Slavic *tajьnъ. By surface analysis, taină + -ic.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic таина (taina), from Proto-Slavic *tajьna. Compare Bulgarian тайна (tajna), Czech tajemství, Polish tajemnica, Russian тайна (tajna), Serbo-Croatian tajna.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тѣскъ (těskŭ), from Proto-Slavic *těskъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic телѣга (telěga), from Proto-Slavic *telěga. Cognates include Russian телега (telega), Czech taliha, Serbo-Croatian таљиге.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тьмьница (tĭmĭnica), from Proto-Slavic *tьmьnica, from *tьmьnъ + *-ica, from *tьma + *-ьnъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *timāˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *temH-.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic *тѣсковина (*těskovina), from тѣскъ (těskŭ) + -овъ (-ovŭ) + -ина (-ina), from Proto-Slavic *těskъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тесла (tesla), from Proto-Slavic *tesla.

parole.significato: to cut obliquely a piece of wood
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тесати (tesati), from Proto-Slavic *tesati (“to hew”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тихнѫти (tixnǫti), from тихъ (tixŭ), from Proto-Slavic *tixъ (“quiet”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тина (tina), from Proto-Slavic *tina, cognate with Bulgarian тиня (tinja).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тиса (tisa), from Proto-Slavic *tisa.

parole.significato: to blunt, dull, wear down, grind away at
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic точити (točiti), from Proto-Slavic *točiti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тъкъмити (tŭkŭmiti), from Proto-Slavic *tъkъmiti. Compare Serbo-Croatian takmiti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic топити (topiti), from Proto-Slavic *topiti. Compare Serbo-Croatian topiti, Bulgarian топя (topja).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic топлица (toplica), from топлъ (toplŭ) + -ица (-ica), from Proto-Slavic *toplъ (“warm”) + *-ica (“deadjectival suffix”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic топоръ (toporŭ), from Proto-Slavic *toporъ, from an Iranian language. Also found in Aromanian as tãpor.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic топорище (toporište), from Proto-Slavic *toporište, from *toporъ (“axe”) + *-ište.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic трѣба (trěba), from Proto-Slavic *terba. Compare Bulgarian трябва (trjabva), Serbo-Croatian treba.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic трѣзвъ (trězvŭ), from Proto-Slavic *terzvъ (“sober”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic трѣбьникъ (trěbĭnikŭ), from трѣба (trěba) + -ьникъ (-ĭnikŭ), from Proto-Slavic *terba.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тръстиѥ (trŭstije, “reed”), from Proto-Slavic *trъstьje, from *trъstь.

parole.significato: third (preceding a medieval rank in Wallachia or Moldavia)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic третии (tretii), from Proto-Slavic *tretь.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic троскотъ (troskotŭ), from Proto-Slavic *torskotъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic троудити (truditi), from Proto-Slavic *truditi, from *trudъ (“labour”) + *-iti (denominal suffix).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic троудьнъ (trudĭnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *trudьnъ, from *trudъ (“labour, effort”) + *-ьnъ. By surface analysis, trudă + -nic.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic троудъ (trudŭ), from Proto-Slavic *trudъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic троупъ (trupŭ), from Proto-Slavic *trupъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic трѫбица (trǫbica), diminutive of трѫба (trǫba), from Proto-Slavic *trǫba. Doublet of Turbuța.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic трѫтити (trǫtiti), from Proto-Slavic *trǫtiti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тоулити (tuliti), with senses from затулити (zatuliti, “to hide”), from Proto-Slavic *tuliti. Compare Bulgarian туля (tulja).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тлъкъ (tlŭkŭ), from Proto-Slavic *tъlkъ. Compare Slovak tĺk.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тлъковати (tlŭkovati, “to explain, to interpret”), from Proto-Slavic *tъlkovati, from *tъlkъ (“interpretation”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тѫпъ (tǫpŭ), from Proto-Slavic *tǫpъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тѫговати (tǫgovati), from тѫга (tǫga), from Proto-Slavic *tǫga (“sadness”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тѫжити (tǫžiti), from тѫга (tǫga, “sadness, melancholy”), from Proto-Slavic *tǫga. Not related to tânjală.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic трьти (trĭti), from Proto-Slavic *terti. Compare Serbo-Croatian trti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тлъмачь (tlŭmačĭ), from Proto-Slavic *tъlmačь (“interpreter”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тлъмачити (tlŭmačiti), from Proto-Slavic *tъlmačiti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic оученикъ (učenikŭ, “disciple, apprentice”), from Proto-Slavic *učenikъ. Compare Russian ученик (učenik), Serbo-Croatian učenik.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic олѣи (olěi), from Proto-Slavic *olějь, itself borrowed from Latin oleum or Ancient Greek ἔλαιον (élaion). Doublet of oleu, oleum, and oloi.

parole.significato: lane (narrow passageway between fences or walls)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic оулица (ulica), from Proto-Slavic *ulica. Compare Serbo-Croatian ulica, Aromanian ulitsã.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ѫдица (ǫdica), from Proto-Slavic *ǫdica.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ѫгри (ǫgri), from Proto-Slavic *ǫgrinъ.

parole.significato: unit of measurement for liquids (around 10 liters)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic вѣдро (vědro), from Proto-Slavic *vědro (“bucket”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic валъ (valŭ), from Proto-Slavic *valъ. Compare Serbo-Croatian val; close to Albanian valë.
From Old Church Slavonic варъ (varŭ), from Proto-Slavic *varъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic вѣкъ (věkŭ), from Proto-Slavic *věkъ. Compare Serbo-Croatian vek.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic видѣние (viděnije), from Proto-Slavic *viděnьje, from *viděti. By surface analysis, vedea + -enie.

parole.significato: great (preceding a medieval rank in Wallachia or Moldavia)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic велии (velii), from Proto-Slavic *velь.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic верига (veriga), from Proto-Slavic *veriga.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic веселъ (veselŭ), from Proto-Slavic *veselъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic вѣсть (věstĭ, “news, message”), from Proto-Slavic *věstь. Compare Russian весть (vestʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic вѣтрило (větrilo), from Proto-Slavic *větridlo.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic вѣверица (věverica), from Proto-Slavic *věverica, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wer-. Compare Aromanian viviritsã.
From older form vecinic, from Old Church Slavonic вѣчьнъ (věčĭnŭ, “eternal”), from Proto-Slavic *věčьnъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic вꙑдра (vydra), from Proto-Slavic *vydra, from Proto-Indo-European *údreh₂. Doublet of lutră.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic вихъръ (vixŭrŭ, “windstorm”), from Proto-Slavic *vixъrъ. Compare Serbo-Croatian vihor.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic вина (vina, “guilt”), from Proto-Slavic *vina.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic *витѧѕь (*vitędzĭ), from Proto-Slavic *vitędzь. Doublet of viking.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic влахъ (vlaxŭ), from Proto-Slavic *volxъ, itself of Germanic origin. Doublet of valah and olah.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic власть (vlastĭ), from Proto-Slavic *volstь.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic воѥвода (vojevoda), from Proto-Slavic *vojevoda.

parole.significato: hale, healthy, sturdy, robust, vigorous, stout
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic воиникъ (voinikŭ, “warrior”), from Proto-Slavic *vojьnikъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic вольнъ (volĭnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *volьnъ, from *volъ (“sufficiency”) + *-ьnъ (adjectival suffix).

parole.significato: official in charge with justice and internal affairs in the Principality of Moldavia
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic дворьникъ (dvorĭnikŭ), from Proto-Slavic *dvorьnikъ, from *dvorъ (“court”) + *-nikъ. Compare Russian дворник (dvornik), Slovak nádvorník, Hungarian nádor.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic врабии (vrabii), from Proto-Slavic *vorbь. Compare Serbo-Croatian vrabac, Russian воробе́й (vorobéj).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic вражьда (vražĭda), from Proto-Slavic *voržьda. Compare Bulgarian вражда (vražda), Russian вражда (vražda).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic вража (vraža), from Proto-Slavic *voržь. Cognate with Serbo-Croatian vraža.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic хврастъ (xvrastŭ), from Proto-Slavic *xvorstъ (“brushwood”). Compare Bulgarian храст (hrast), Serbo-Croatian hrast, Russian хворост (xvorost).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic врѣдьнъ (vrědĭnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *verdьnъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic врѣмѧ (vrěmę), from Proto-Slavic *vermę. Compare Megleno-Romanian vreami, Bulgarian време (vreme), Serbo-Croatian vreme, Russian время (vremja).
From vânj + -os, from Old Church Slavonic вѫзъ (vǫzŭ), from Proto-Slavic *vǫzъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic врьхъ (vrĭxŭ), from Proto-Slavic *vьrxъ. Compare Serbo-Croatian vrh. First attested in the 16th century.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic врьста (vrĭsta), from Proto-Slavic *vьrsta.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic врътежь (vrŭtežĭ), from врьтѣти (vrĭtěti, “to turn around”) + -ежь (-ežĭ), from Proto-Slavic *vьrtěti. A link to Latin vertigium is highly improbable.

parole.significato: to thrust, poke or shove into
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic врѣти (vrěti), from Proto-Slavic *vèrti. Compare Bulgarian вра́ (vrá).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic весло (veslo), from Proto-Slavic *veslo.

parole.significato: to show clearly, bring to light, make clear or apparent, indicate, betoken, bewray
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic вадити (vaditi), from Proto-Slavic *vaditi.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic въздоухъ (vŭzduxŭ), from Proto-Slavic *vъzduxъ. Compare Russian воздух (vozdux).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic за (za) + даръ (darŭ), from Proto-Slavic *za + *darъ (“gift”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic записъ (zapisŭ), from писати (pisati), from Proto-Slavic *pisati, from Proto-Indo-European *peyḱ- (“to paint, draw”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic зависть (zavistĭ, “envy”), from Proto-Slavic *zavistь.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic завистьникъ (zavistĭnikŭ, “envious person”), from зависть (zavistĭ, “envy”) + -ьникъ (-ĭnikŭ), from за- (za-) + видѣти (viděti, “to see”), from Proto-Slavic *viděti (“to see”). Compare Russian завистник (zavistnik).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съборъ (sŭborŭ), from Proto-Slavic *sъborъ (“meeting, gathering”). Doublet of sobor.

parole.significato: sturdy, tough, healthy, sound, whole, sane, vigorous, mighty
parole.testo: From Old Church Slavonic съдравъ (sŭdravŭ), from Proto-Slavic *sъdravьnъ. Compare zdravo.

parole.significato: wall (generally outside, as in the wall of a building)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic зьдъ (zĭdŭ), from Proto-Slavic *zidъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic зьдати (zĭdati), from Proto-Slavic *zьdati (“to build”).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic слота (slota), from Proto-Slavic *slota. Compare Bulgarian слота (slota), Serbo-Croatian slota, Czech slota, Slovak slota, Polish słota, Ukrainian сльота (slʹota), Belarusian слота (slóta).

parole.significato: evil giant in Romanian folk stories
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic змиꙗ (zmija), from Proto-Slavic *zmьja (“snake”). Compare Serbo-Croatian zmija and zmaj.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic зорꙗ (zorja), from Proto-Slavic *zořa. See also zare. Compare Bulgarian зора (zora), Serbo-Croatian zora, Aromanian ndzari.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic звонъ (zvonŭ), from Proto-Slavic *zvonъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic зѫбъ (zǫbŭ), from Proto-Slavic *zǫbъ (“tooth”), cf. Bulgarian зъбя се (zăbja se).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic забава (zabava), from Proto-Slavic *zabava.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic забовити (zaboviti), from Proto-Slavic *zabava.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic забрало (zabralo), from Proto-Slavic *zaborlo, from *borniti (“to prevent, to defend”).

parole.significato: forest by the banks of a river
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic завои (zavoi), from Proto-Slavic *zavojь (“bend, turn”), from *vojь. Compare Serbo-Croatian zavoj, Bulgarian завой (zavoj).
în + zadar, derived from Old Church Slavonic за (za) + даръ (darŭ), from Proto-Slavic *za + *darъ (“gift”).
From în- + Old Church Slavonic дрьзнѫти (drĭznǫti), from Proto-Slavic *dьrznǫti.

parole.significato: to enclose, fence in, block up, wall in
parole.testo: From în- + Old Church Slavonic градити (graditi), from Proto-Slavic *gorditi.

parole.significato: murmur (of water, of wind, of leaves)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic шьпотъ (šĭpotŭ), from Proto-Slavic *šьpъtъ. Compare Serbo-Croatian šapat, Bulgarian шепот (šepot).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic шъптати (šŭptati), from Proto-Slavic *šьpъtati. Compare Bulgarian шептя (šeptja).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic штавь (štavĭ), from Proto-Slavic *štavъ (“sorrel”).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic доушегоубьць (dušegubĭcĭ, “killer, seducer of the soul, killer of the soul”), from Proto-Slavic *dušegubьcь, from *duša (“soul”) + *gubiti (“to destroy”). Compare Russian душегубец (dušegubec, “killer”), Bulgarian душегубец (dušegubec),
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic шоуи (šui), from Proto-Slavic *šujь (“left”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic шоумьнъ (šumĭnŭ, “tipsy”), from Proto-Slavic *šumьnъ (“noisy”), from *šumъ (“noise”).
